in writing. − the european union has taken important steps to protect copyright. one example is the suite directive, which created the right of the author to participate in the resale procedure of the work. in this way, the fair treatment of authors as provided for by the berne convention was ensured. the application of the directive in all member states as from 1 january 2012 will bring even greater benefits. i believe that the implementation of the suite right provisions is essential to have a single copyright market. the potential of the union market for artistic, visual and graphic works is very high for both authors and consumers. therefore, the protection and respect of copyright holders must remain a crucial objective of the union in stimulating innovation and creation.
in writing. - i voted for the report on the implementation of the right of suite. artistic creation contributes to the continuous development of the eu's cultural life and heritage. in 2011, the european art market experienced a sharp increase. the united kingdom has a market share of 19,4% of the world market, with a 24% increase in sales volume; france has a market share of 4.5%, with a turnover growth of 9%, and germany, with a market share of 1.8% (3), has seen sales increase by 23%. many of the provisions of the directive ensure a balanced application of the suite right, taking into account the interests of all interested parties, in particular the gradual reduction of the applicable rates, the capping of the right at eur 12 500, the exclusion of small sales and the granting of exemptions in the case of resales to the first purchaser. i would point out, however, that the directive imposes an administrative burden on traders. calls on the commission to carry out an assessment of the impact of the functioning of the art market in general, including the administrative difficulties faced by smaller and specialist auction houses and art dealers.
in writing. - i voted in favour of the report because i believe it is important that parliament's rules of procedure, especially as regards interinstitutional negotiations, be adapted to the current context. the revision of article 70 of the rules of procedure with a view to increasing the effectiveness, transparency and inclusiveness of the procedures by including some of the key elements of the code of conduct for negotiations under the ordinary legislative procedure in the mandatory part of the rules of procedure is welcomed. in cases of urgency, it is necessary that a commission with competence in the matter be able to conduct negotiations and update the mandate on the basis of developments. a too strict definition in the regulation of the form of such a mandate would be counterproductive in terms of flexibility and efficiency.
in writing. - i voted in favour of parliament's decision amending rule 70 of parliament's rules of procedure on interinstitutional negotiations in the context of legislative procedures. rule 70 of the rules of procedure is useful when the three institutions - parliament, the commission and the council - are negotiating legislative acts of interest to the eu. negotiations with the other institutions with a view to reaching an agreement in the course of a legislative procedure shall be conducted taking into account the code of conduct established by the conference of presidents. negotiations shall be opened only after the committee responsible for each legislative procedure concerned has, on a case-by-case basis and by a majority of its component members, adopted a decision to open negotiations. that decision shall determine the mandate and composition of the negotiating team. the mandate shall consist of a report adopted in committee and tabled for further consideration by parliament. the negotiating team shall be headed by the rapporteur and chaired by the chair of the committee responsible or by a vice-chair designated by the chair. the team shall include at least the alternate rapporteurs from each political group. any decision by a committee to open negotiations before adoption of a report in committee shall be translated into all the official languages, distributed to all members of parliament and forwarded to the conference of presidents.
in writing. - i voted in favour of the report because i believe that it is necessary to continue to maintain a system whereby decisions and debates in the european parliament are accessible to citizens of the union, irrespective of their nationality and language. the provision of the shorthand in their original language will result in greater budgetary and resource savings and at the same time allow the principle of multilingualism to be maintained. this is particularly important to preserve the cultural and linguistic identity of each citizen, but also to avoid creating certain hierarchies in relation to the official languages of the union. the amendments will also not affect the simultaneous translation system, which will continue to be provided in all official languages of the union.
in writing. - i voted to amend rule 181 of parliament's rules of procedure on the transcripts of debates and rule 182 on the audio-visual recording of debates. in the context of the current economic and financial crisis, parliament wanted to implement a package of cost-cutting measures for the 2012 budget. the minutes of meetings will therefore be compiled exclusively in the form of a multilingual document in which all the speeches appear only in their original language, with no automatic translation being provided. the provision of the stenograms exclusively in their original language will result in budgetary savings and, at the same time, allow the principle of multilingualism to be maintained. oral contributions are in their original language and speakers may make corrections to the text of their oral contributions within five working days. parliament's debates are also broadcast in real time on its website in the languages in which they are held, together with the multilingual soundtrack of all active interpretation booths. immediately after each sitting, an indexed audio-visual recording of the debates in the languages in which they were held, together with the multilingual audio-tape of all active interpreting booths, shall be made available to the public on parliament's website for the duration of the current and the next parliamentary term, after which it shall be kept in parliament's archives.
in writing. - i voted in favour of the proposal for a regulation on the approval and market surveillance of two- or three-wheel vehicles and quadricycles. the regulation aims to establish harmonised rules for the type-approval of l-category vehicles with a view to ensuring the functioning of the internal market. l-category vehicles are two, three or four-wheel vehicles (motorcycles, tricycles and quadricycles). the regulation aims to simplify the existing legal framework, reduce emissions from l-category vehicles, increase the overall level of safety and strengthen the rules on market surveillance. for reasons of clarity, predictability, rationalisation and simplification, and in order to reduce the burden on vehicle manufacturers, this regulation should contain a limited number of implementation steps for the introduction of new emission levels and safety requirements. sufficient time should be allowed for the industry to adapt to the new provisions laid down in this regulation. timely definition of the requirements is essential to ensure sufficient time for manufacturers to develop, test and implement technical solutions for series-produced vehicles and for manufacturers and approval authorities in the member states to put in place the necessary administrative systems.
in writing. − i welcome the objective of this legislative proposal to establish harmonised rules for the manufacture of agricultural and forestry vehicles, so that the existing legislation on vehicle type-approval is simplified.
in writing. - i voted in favour of the proposal for a regulation on the type-approval of agricultural and forestry vehicles. it lays down the requirements for the market surveillance of vehicles, systems, components and separate technical units approved under this regulation. it also lays down requirements for the market surveillance of parts and equipment intended for such vehicles. the union is a contracting party to the agreement of the united nations economic commission for europe (unece) concerning the adoption of uniform technical specifications for wheeled vehicles, equipment and components which can be fitted to and/or be used on wheeled vehicles and the conditions for reciprocal recognition of approvals granted on the basis of these specifications. in order to simplify the type-approval legislation, it is appropriate to repeal all individual directives without reducing the level of protection. the requirements laid down in those directives should be taken over in this regulation or in the delegated acts adopted pursuant to this regulation and, where appropriate, replaced by references to the relevant unece regulations. in order to reduce the administrative burden of the type-approval process, vehicle manufacturers should be allowed to apply for type-approval in accordance with this regulation.

in writing. - i voted for the resolution 'towards an integrated european market for card, internet and mobile payments'. the proportion and variety of internet and mobile payments is constantly growing in europe and worldwide, and i believe it is important to remove the obstacles to a fully integrated european digital single market that is competitive, innovative, safe, transparent and consumer-friendly in these forms of payments. i believe that common technical standards based on open access would improve the competitiveness of the european economy and the functioning of the internal market, promote interoperability and also bring security benefits in the form of common security standards, which would benefit consumers and traders alike. i believe that the minimum security requirements for internet, card and mobile payments should be the same in all member states and that there should be a common regulatory body to set these requirements. i would stress that standardised security solutions would simplify customer information and thus be the way for customers to adapt to security systems, which would reduce costs for payment service providers (psps).
in writing. − i believe that there is a need for stricter monitoring of entities that perform banking-like functions but are outside the regulatory system. the shadow banking system is considered to be one of the triggers of the global financial crisis. it is closely linked to the regular banking system, which raises many concerns about systemic risks. i voted in favour of the report on shadow banking because i believe that no actor or financial instrument should be left out of the rules. we need more stable, more efficient financial markets geared towards stimulating the real economy.
in writing. − i voted in favour of the european parliament resolution on shadow banking (sbp) because the shadow banking sector plays an important role in the financial system. the parallel banking system, as defined by the financial stability board (fsb), refers to the credit intermediation system involving entities and activities outside the traditional banking system. regulated entities within the traditional banking system participate significantly in the activities defined as part of the shadow banking system and are interconnected in many ways with shadow banking entities. parallel banking creates new sources of funding and offers investors alternatives to bank deposits, but it can also entail potential risks to long-term financial stability. we voted to increase the reliability of bank balance sheets and we ask the commission to come up with a legislative proposal to separate the personal and investment activities of banks. we call on the commission to carry out, in future, comprehensive impact studies on the effects of each legislative proposal on the financing of the real economy.
in writing. − children are the most exposed group to risks when surfing the internet. their thirst for knowledge can often turn them into victims of psychological manipulation, child pornography, invasion of privacy, online gambling, commercial fraud, and more. i believe that minors need to be protected when they are in cyberspace by promoting digital education and training at european level for children, parents, educators, school teachers and social workers, so that they understand the digital world and identify the dangers to which this age group is exposed when using the internet. i believe it is important to ensure the continuity of the 'safer internet' programme, which provides funding for programmes aimed at increasing the level of protection of minors in cyberspace, in an increasingly effective and collaborative way at european level. i voted in favour of this report.

in writing. the european union's dependence on energy imports, in particular oil and, more recently, natural gas, is a major concern in the energy policy field, for reasons of security of energy supply. the decline in primary natural gas production has led to an increase in the eu's dependence on primary energy imports, with over 60% of the gas the union consumes today being imported. a study on geological resources published in may 2012 shows that natural gas could account for 25% of the world's energy resources. shale gas is a resource that no eu country can afford to neglect. according to the us government's energy information agency, european shale gas reserves amount to 18 000 billion cubic metres, a figure that is not negligible for the european continent. of course, the environmental impact of the exploitation of these gases must be taken into account, but the technologies used today worldwide can allow efficient exploitation, including in terms of environmental protection. a rational exploitation would have a dual purpose: to reduce the eu's dependence on gas imports, but also to create new jobs and horizontal industrial development.
i appreciate the european commission's proactive approach to the impact of the anticipated restructuring on the automotive industry. the crisis has taught us something, it has reminded us of a truth: that industry is extremely important for the soundness of the european economy, and the automobile industry is important for the european industrial base. not only does it create jobs in the countries where cars are assembled, it creates jobs through the supply chain in all member states. for example, no car today comes off a production line in germany without containing, for example, parts produced in romania. but the automobile industry is in global competition. it is a global industry, under strong global competition, and a european or a national policy can sustain or kill the competitiveness of this industry. if we look at it, there is no member state in the european union that is similar to another member state in terms of the tax regime for pollution, car registration taxes and so on, and these differences are obstacles to the development of the european automobile industry, obstacles to the single market. is there nothing we can do to harmonize the little things, to eliminate these differences? in the united states, as in other countries, governments have given substantial aid to the automobile industry to innovate, to move to lower carbon dioxide cars. we need to do the same.
at the moment, the whole of european industry is going through a difficult period and the outlook is not encouraging at all. this is all the more true in the automobile industry. competitiveness in this sector needs to be boosted, and the action plan adopted by the commission to this end focuses precisely on innovation and making the necessary investments in this area. the plan addresses both internal and external issues and aims to regulate and relaunch the sector. market conditions must be improved and the automotive industry must be given more support on the world market. as for my country, romania has the capacity to produce cars with cutting-edge industrial technology, and the new dacia models confirm this. the role of the egf has become more important in the context of the crisis, providing support to employees in the sector.
in writing. the steel industry accounts for 1.4% of european gdp. the restructuring of the european steel industry, together with the increase in steel imports from third countries, not subject to the same stringent environmental regulations, led to job losses in europe. thus, the steel workforce decreased from 1 million employees in 1970 to around 408 000 employees in 2008. in 2010, eu steel exports amounted to 33,7 million tonnes, the main importers being turkey, the usa, algeria, switzerland, russia and india, and union steel imports were 26,8 million tonnes, the main exporters being russia (6,5 million tonnes), ukraine (5,7 million tonnes), china (3,6 million tonnes), turkey (1,8 million tonnes), south korea, switzerland and serbia. against the background of the economic crisis, the steel industry in romania, belgium, sweden and bulgaria was the most affected. steel is the most widely used material in the world, due to its strength, flexibility and multiple uses, with production reaching 1.4 billion tonnes in 2010. the union needs a competitive steel industry capable of providing jobs throughout europe. i call on the commission and the member states to support the european steel industry to modernise, as it is only by becoming less polluting and more energy efficient that it can remain internationally competitive.
he is seeking the presidency of the council. - the the second generation schengen information system (sis ii) is a key tool for the security of the european area without internal border controls and one of the most tangible and important achievements of european integration. sis ii will replace the existing system, which has the capacity to serve the needs of a limited number of member states and to respond to a limited number of requests. improved technology gives the new schengen information system new functions and enables it to respond to a greater number of requests, thus enhancing the security of the schengen area and its citizens. in may 2012, the european commission presented its proposal for a revision of the two existing legal acts governing the transition from schengen i+ to the new sis ii. the presidency, aware that this is a necessary element of the transition process, has worked intensively to ensure that work proceeds quickly so that agreement can be reached on the text of the proposal. the debate on the council proposal resulted in a change in the legal structure of the original commission proposal in order to bring it into line with the usual practice for legal proposals involving ireland and the united kingdom and to ensure a more transparent procedure. the presidency would like to thank the rapporteur of the european parliament and the european parliament for all the efforts they have made to ensure the timely and rapid adoption of the reports on the proposals, thus enabling the council to proceed with their final adoption. as you will have generally understood, the responsibility for the development and completion of sis ii has been taken over by the european commission and the deadline for the operational operation of the system is still the end of the first quarter of 2013, according to the latest overall timetable drawn up by the european commission. the adoption of the legal proposals governing the transition will be another essential step towards the objective of sis ii becoming operational in the first quarter of 2013. this also requires that both the central and all national systems should be ready by the aforementioned time period. the european commission regularly informs the council of the state of progress of sis ii and a further update is expected at the justice and home affairs council on 6 and 7 december. i hope that by then it will be clear whether the target of completing the system by the end of march 2013 remains achievable.
vice-president of the commission. − mr president, sis ii is a major milestone in the completion of the area of freedom, security and justice. i look forward to what i hope will be a positive vote tomorrow on the migration instrument recast proposal. this is essential in laying down both the migration procedure and the underlying legal framework, and is indispensable for sis ii to become operational. i would like to thank the rapporteur, mr coelho, and the civil liberties committee for their constructive spirit and cooperation throughout the procedure. the commission aims to guarantee the highest level of data protection throughout the migration. the proposal by the european parliament in this area provides further clarity and can, therefore, be strongly supported by the commission. the commission regards data cleansing as a priority and has on several occasions made member states aware of the crucial importance of this issue in order to avoid substantial numbers of rejected alerts by the new system. on this basis, the commission can also support the relevant amendments put forward in the reports. in order to enhance transparency, the commission is ready to provide the european parliament with information about the testing activities laid down in the proposal as well as about the completion of the migration. under article 18 of the migration instruments, the commission will deliver progress reports to the european parliament and to the council every six months concerning the technical development of sis ii and migration-related activities. however, the commission cannot support the inclusion of requirements obliging member states to delete non-migrated data, as these data are subject to national law and the supervision of the national data protection authorities in accordance with the schengen convention. undeniable progress has been made in the sis ii project over the last two years at both central and national level. the commission has already informed the parliament of the successful completion of the milestone 2 test earlier this year and of the very good performance of the central system and most national systems during the last round of testing, known as the comprehensive test. so i would like to underline the fact that we are actually very close to completion. this is unfortunately not the case for finland, where there has been a slight delay in completing its national system. the finnish authorities notified the commission of this in late october in a letter from the finnish interior minister. commissioner malmström raised this issue as an urgent matter for finland to address at the justice and home affairs (jha) council a few days later. immediately after the jha council, the commission organised a fact-finding mission to finland to assess the extent of the difficulties encountered by their national project. a number of risk mitigation actions were agreed with finland, which could, alongside the assistance that will be provided to their experts, minimise the impact on the overall project schedule but cannot prevent some delay. the commission’s services are analysing in detail the implications of the problem encountered by finland. on the basis of the detailed information requested from finland on its remedial action plan, the commission’s intention is to present a new timetable to the december jha council on 6 and 7 december 2012 and, of course, to inform the parliament at the same time.
the reports we are debating tonight on migration to sis ii were adopted in the libe committee by a simplified procedure, in order to make available to the commission and the member states as soon as possible both the legal instruments and the funds needed to move to the new generation of sis. this spirit of good faith and cooperation of parliament unfortunately stands in stark contrast to the attitude of some member states which show a lack of interest in the success of sis ii. i sincerely share my personal frustration, but also that of the whole european parliament, with regard to this endless problem of the schengen ii information system. it is already ridiculous that an information system, even if complex, should take more than 12 years to develop and implement and even now the member states and the commission cannot keep their commitments and repeat the mistakes of the past. in this case, there is a worrying lack of responsibility, both on the part of finland, which shows a lack of interest in carrying out simple tests, and on the part of the commission. the basic condition imposed by parliament on the commission for the release of funds for the development of sis ii was its commitment to respect and closely monitor the migration process. unfortunately, the commission has not kept its commitment. all of this once again highlights the reasons why the whole management of the schengen area must be changed and europeanised. if we had an effective community assessment mechanism, all these delays could have been avoided and much more prompt action could have been taken to correct problems such as finland's. finally, i would like to note the irony of the situation where romania and bulgaria, candidate countries which, although they fulfil all the requirements of the acquis to access the schengen area, are not accepted to join, and an old schengen member state has serious problems with respecting the acquis.
vice-president of the commission. − mr president, i thank members for all their comments. i assure you that i have taken good note of the concerns expressed in the debate, and i can tell you that the commission shares many of them. despite the delay, we are very, very close to completion of the sis ii project. the central system amply proved its robustness to the satisfaction of the vast majority of the member states, and the project has now reached the point of no return. the objective of bringing the system into operation as soon as possible remains, therefore, an imperative which must not be compromised. experience shows that this is only possible through overall constructive cooperation and solidarity promoted by all the stakeholders. the commission is further ready to provide any possible support needed to overcome all the remaining challenges. the added value that sis ii will bring to our common area of freedom and security merits our utmost engagement to ensure the final delivery. many of your comments and worries have centred on the fact that we witnessed a delay in the readiness of finland, and baroness ludford asked why the problem had not been detected earlier. here i would like to emphasise that the monitoring system for national development, namely the sis ii task force, was put in place by the council some time ago but it obviously failed to detect the technical issues arising in finland. as you know, the member states bear full responsibility for the system at their level, and given that finland did not volunteer for an earlier testing campaign, the national issues there were revealed only in the last round of tests, which were mandatory for all member states. at the same time, i believe this is still an issue which we can solve together because now we have cooperation with finland, and the commission and the other member states are making efforts to assist as much as possible. i believe that, with all the other member states, the migration will start as planned in january, and finland will join these efforts once it is ready. concerning the complete switchover, we have to wait until the whole system is ready, but i believe that we are really very close to that point and we will do our utmost to have a clear answer for you after thorough examination of the issue and the discussion among the interior ministers on 5 and 6 once the system is in place and operational, we will all benefit from the high quality of reliable services and the new information which we will be able to obtain, and i think it will further improve the way we actually use the freedoms we have as citizens, including freedom of travel.

vice-president of the commission. − mr president, i would first like to thank the rapporteur, mr chichester, for his work in drafting this valuable report as well as ms mazzoni and the whole petitions committee, whose impressive work is reflected in this report. the report points to some of the most topical and sensitive areas subject to the citizens’ petition in the field of environment and fundamental rights, on which the commission and parliament are already working closely and will continue to exchange information and views. today’s debate marks a good opportunity to underline my appreciation of parliament’s remarkable commitment to the smooth implementation of article 227 of the treaty, which reserves the right of any eu citizen resident in the member state or any company, organisation, association with its headquarters in the eu to submit a petition to the european parliament. the commission is particularly happy to be able to contribute to parliament’s important work. this is a considerable investment in terms of resources. and it is worth it, since handling the citizen’s petitions is ultimately also a means for the eu institutions of winning citizens’ trust in these difficult times. in this regard, the european parliament and the commission clearly share the commitment to put citizens first. citizens are and must always remain at the centre of all our activities and discussions. as rightly mentioned in the lichtenberger report, which is the next point on this plenary session’s agenda, the committee on petitions plays a central role as an effective link between citizens, the parliament and the commission. this is why the commission always includes a section on petitions in its annual report on the application of the eu law, in which we recognise that petitions to the european parliament lead to infringement proceedings in a number of areas. in the next annual report on the application of eu law, which will be adopted in the coming weeks, we also plan to indicate the concrete number of cases which had their origin in petitions. with this in mind, please let me reiterate our willing and continued collaboration with your work on parliament’s committee on petitions. as mr chichester’s report points out, you asked us for help with over half of the almost 1000 admissible petitions which you received in 2011. although our help initially consists mainly in analysing what eu law, if any, might be applicable in the case, we also attend the follow-up meetings of your petitions. it is important that my fellow members of the commission continue to attend key meetings for exchanges of views with your committee. allow me to say a few words on the european citizens’ initiative, a system in which the petitions committee has a relevant role. since 1 april 2012 a new tool of participatory democracy has been in place at eu level with the entry into application of the european citizens’ initiative. the initial technical problems encountered are being solved. the commission has put its own servers at the disposal of organisers and provided extended help, guidance and assistance to them for the certification process. three initiatives are now up and running, collecting signatures on-line even as we speak. i would like to assure you that i am committed to making sure that citizens can make full use of their new rights, and i look forward to our cooperation in that regard. i would like to conclude by stressing that the commission looks forward to continuing and enhancing its fruitful cooperation with parliament’s petitions committee.
on behalf of the epp group. as you know, the committee on petitions does not appear very often on the agenda of the plenary. however, the work of this committee is extremely important. it is about accepting citizens' grievances, and in this context, it is about defending the rights of european citizens. this is why the committee holds a large number of hearings each year. this is also why we maintain a close dialogue with the european commission, the member states and other bodies and institutions such as the european ombudsman. unfortunately, almost half of the petitions submitted are still inadmissible because they concern matters which are outside the union's competence, and i therefore believe that it is very good from now on to provide citizens with additional information about the union in general and parliament in particular. i also believe that the involvement of the committee on petitions in organising hearings on proposed european citizens' initiatives, which commissioner šefčovič also mentioned, can make a positive contribution to this information process. i would also like to say that, apart from the countries mentioned by mr chichester last year, germany, spain and italy, as the first in the order of petitions, poland and romania are next, which shows us that both citizens of the old member states and citizens of the new member states are involved in defending their rights at european level. the main topics covered by the petitions are: environmental protection, the internal market, fundamental rights, not coincidentally, because these are fundamental areas of the union. i would like to conclude my brief speech by saying that i support the effective and appropriate use of this instrument which serves to establish a direct dialogue between parliament and the citizens.
on behalf of the s&d group. let me begin by congratulating the rapporteur, mr chichester, on his excellent report and on the excellent cooperation we have had during the drafting and committee debates. as in previous years, the committee on petitions received a very large number of petitions concerning infringements of european environmental legislation. once again, i would ask the member states to attach particular importance to these matters. the quality of the daily lives of european citizens and the preservation of our union's unique natural heritage are both at stake. in this context, i welcome commissioner potočnik's initiative to come up with an amendment to the directive on 'environmental impact assessment' and i would like to underline the contribution that the committee on petitions has made to this development. i ask that this change be made in the first place by taking account of clear, transparent criteria and guaranteeing the neutrality and objectivity of impact studies, given that these are the major weaknesses of the present directive. our commission has been and is a place where european citizens express their concerns about the non-respect of european rights. the only amendment tabled by the s&d group goes in that direction. on behalf of the european citizens and myself, i call today on all member states and the european commission to respect the freedom of movement for all european citizens, regardless of nationality, race or sexual orientation.
as vice-chair of the committee on petitions, i have come to the conclusion that petitioning can be the best method of bringing to the public's attention the problems faced by ordinary citizens in the face of injustices by the authorities. in 2011, the majority of petitions were related to fundamental rights issues. one thing i do not agree with and hope that in the future this will be corrected is that too many petitions contain political subjects which are, in any case, national and not community competence and which should not be declared admissible from the outset. some examples would be topics such as: freedom of the press, cyanide mining in rosia montana, community dogs and, more recently, shale gas exploitation. i hope that in future the admissibility of such petitions will be more thoroughly analysed, that it will be clearer when political issues on the agenda of a member state are brought before the committee on petitions. as with the peti commission visit to romania, the same thing is happening with most documentary visits to other member states. as members of parliament, we each belong to a political party, but we should use this committee only in the interests of the citizens and not to serve the interests of the party, to attack or defend the government in power in a member state.
to move forward in the process of integration, it is not enough to adopt community legislation. its implementation is also important, and the 2010 report shows that there are major shortcomings at the level of some member states. romania is not, and in 2010 it only appeared before the court of justice once. although the number of cases brought against my country increased in 2010, the authorities were able to remedy the deficiencies before they reached the court. it is an example of effective cooperation between the commission and the romanian authorities. another important point in the report is the role of petitions in monitoring the application of community law. they are a great way for citizens to draw attention to breaches of european rules, and early resolution of problems can also reduce the risk of a member state being brought before the court.
this is the first time that the multiannual financial framework has been discussed under the lisbon treaty. unfortunately, the provisions of the treaty have created difficulties and, in my view, diminish the democratic character of the adoption of the budget. the approval procedure for the mff and the codecision procedure for horizontal policies are contradictory, not complementary. the european council is not respecting the treaty and is proposing elements that should be negotiated in codecision. the council and parliament were blocked in the co-decision process by imposing a non-negotiation of the resources needed for european policies. the rotating presidency of the european council has drawn up one proposal, the president of the european council another. my opinion: i don't think this is normal. both down on the commission's proposal. in this time of crisis, all member states are increasing their national budget allocations for investment, growth and jobs. the same must be true of the european budget, which is 94% investment budget. the net taxpayers know very well that a euro invested in one region of europe brings benefits to other regions of the union. if there is public money to support the banking system, there must be funds to support european policies that create growth and jobs and, by implication, healthy support for the banking system. the european council endorsed the 2020 strategy - european and national targets. the same council has a duty to ensure that the european budget is adequate to meet these objectives. i think the members of the council have to choose between a populist stance, which means cutting, and a development-oriented stance, because the money will go back to the member states.
i would like to say at the outset that parliament and the european commission are united in defending the interest of europeans in a budget for development and investment and i welcome the contribution of the president of the european commission, mr barroso. i want to say, as rapporteur for the cohesion fund report, that the logic behind president van rompuy's statements and proposal is simply shocking. on the one hand, he says that cohesion policy is aimed at reducing disparities, but then in his documents we find three things that are all against the first thesis: a substantial reduction in the budget for cohesion policy, a reduction in co-financing rates for the least developed regions of the european union and, even more surprisingly, the punishment of regions with a low absorption rate and, on top of all this, the macroeconomic conditionalities that parliament has always rejected. mr van rompuy and the council must understand that we cannot ban the word 'solidarity' in europe and that the european union cannot be a rich and selfish centre and a poor periphery. i am sorry to say to president van rompuy that he has forgotten the role of cohesion policy and, more importantly, the role of the european parliament as co-legislator. if the council comes up with the same unacceptable proposal, parliament has only one chance: to reject this budget, which is basically anti-european.
in writing. the negotiations on the 2014-2020 multiannual financial framework are taking place in a very special context, that of austerity policies in most member states. we're all aware of that. but i would like to stress that despite this, i do not think that the cuts in the european budget for 2014-2020, in the form proposed by the commission, are a good idea. the european budget must be complementary to national budgets, financing joint activities that neutralize as much as possible national austerity. the european budget must be a budget for economic growth, which we so badly need! the union needs a genuine budget, able to respond to the expectations of european citizens towards the eu. we cannot say that we want a high degree of economic, social and territorial cohesion, the deepening of the single market and economic growth, and at the same time cut the budget lines that finance these objectives! i therefore call on the members of the european council to take these matters into account and to take a responsible decision on the cfm so that the eu is not deprived of the financial means necessary to act in its sphere of competence.
in writing. – the eu budget represents a very strong tool to increase strategic investment with european added value and put the european economy back on track, generating growth and employment while aiming to foster economic and social cohesion throughout the eu. it is important to increase funding for employment, education, training, mobility, youth and social inclusion. social inclusion of young europeans has to be mainstreamed and prioritised in all relevant policies financed from the eu budget. youth-related instruments, such as the youth guarantee, have to be proposed by the european commission. the necessary funding for cohesion policy (structural funds and cohesion fund) should remain available for all regions and maintained at least at 2007-13 level. 25 % of the overall funding for cohesion policy should be allocated to esf (european social fund) to promote employability and social investment. 20 % of esf funding should be set aside for promoting social inclusion and combating poverty. european globalisation fund shall be continued and upgraded as in instrument to help all categories of workers to re-enter the labour market and acquire new skills. also, an adequate support for achieving the eu 2020 targets and union objectives for climate, energy, resource-efficiency and biodiversity should be provided.
in writing. the main cause of the deepening of inequalities and the economic crisis in the european union is the greed of some member states and the fact that they often forget the principles of solidarity that govern this union. we need investment in priority areas more than ever, and i believe that cutting budgets for policies that have proven to be very successful, such as cohesion policy and the cap, will seriously damage the eu's economic growth and global competitiveness. for this reason, mr van rompuy's proposal to reduce the budget for cohesion policy by 30 billion euros and the cap by 25 billion euros is unacceptable and the member states must vote against it!
in writing. – the dispute over the multiannual financial framework is not about money but about the future of the eu. it is not about figures but about the political principles generating those figures. a smaller european budget does not mean necessarily better spending, but more likely wasted resources and opportunities. we have to provide the eu with the financial resources necessary for achieving its objectives. any disparity between needs, ambitions and funding is a loss. a bigger eu budget does not mean bigger burdens on the shoulders of the national taxpayers but a better use and distribution of the taxpayers’ money. bigger cohesion funds do not mean that the more productive member states pay for the inefficiency of the less productive states. it means providing opportunities for growth for both more developed and less developed members. solidarity is not charity but the only form of intelligent selfishness in difficult times. on the background of the economic crisis, this framework does not offer solutions for stimulating european solidarity, economic growth or job creation, but rather pushes for national selfishness, absurd austerity and nations’ fragmentation. therefore the council’s draft is unacceptable. parliament and the commission’s positions are the least one could support.
i wanted to speak and explain my vote, which was in favour, because i considered that monitoring the application of union law is one of the important levers by which parliament, the commission and the council can prevent, in some way, the effects of the crisis. in my view, if anything was wrong, it was the way the union treaties were applied, the biased and preferential way in which infringement procedures were initiated. articles 258 and 260 of the treaty on european union provide that all member states are to benefit from this procedure in the event of a breach of the provisions of the treaties. unfortunately, this has not happened, and that is why i believe that a revised regulation is absolutely necessary in principle.

in writing. - i voted in favour of the report on the allocation of tariff quotas for russian timber exports to the eu. in view of the economic importance for the union of imports of raw wood and the importance of the russian federation as a supplier of raw wood to the union, the commission has negotiated commitments with the russian federation that the latter will reduce or eliminate export duties for raw wood. these commitments, which became part of the world trade organisation (wto) list of concessions and commitments on goods of the russian federation upon its accession to the wto, include tariff quotas for the export of certain specified types of coniferous wood, part of which has been allocated to exports to the union. in accordance with the provisions of the agreement, the union shall administer the part of the quota allocated to it in accordance with its internal procedures. decision 2012/105/eu provides that the commission is to adopt detailed rules concerning the method of allocating quota authorisations in accordance with the protocol and any other provisions necessary for the administration by the union of the quantities under the tariff quotas allocated to exports to the union.

in writing. - i voted for the report on the modification of the concessions on processed poultrymeat between the eu and brazil and thailand. following the negotiations under article xxviii of the general agreement on tariffs and trade (gatt) 1994 on poultrymeat, the eu has seen a marked increase in imports of processed poultrymeat. foreign exporters appeared to benefit from a relative difference in the level of protection by reducing the meat/poultry organ content of preparations to a level below 57%, thus qualifying for a close tariff line. as the sharp increase in imports of processed poultry meat has negatively affected the european poultry industry, the commission was authorised by the council to negotiate the modification of the concessions on poultry meat. the commission has been negotiating with brazil and thailand, whose exports would be most affected by the modification of the concessions, each of which has interests as a major supplier. the negotiations resulted in agreements whereby a mutually advantageous countervailing adjustment was agreed to balance the increase in customs duties. the regulation should enter into force on the same date as the two agreements, following the notifications from thailand and brazil.
in writing. - i voted in favour of amending the annexes to protocols 1 and 2 to the euro-mediterranean agreement establishing an association between the ec and israel. in 2005, the council authorised the commission to negotiate with certain mediterranean countries to achieve greater liberalisation of trade in agricultural products, processed agricultural products, fish and fishery products. negotiations with israel were successfully concluded in 2008. the results of those negotiations are incorporated in an agreement in the form of an exchange of letters concerning certain reciprocal liberalisation measures relating to agricultural products, fish and fishery products, replacing protocols 1 and 2 and their annexes, and amending the euro-mediterranean agreement establishing an association between the european communities and their member states, of the one part, and the state of israel, of the other part. following the entry into force of the agreement in the form of an exchange of letters in 2010, the european commission and israel held certain technical meetings related to its implementation. the meetings showed that some technical adjustments are needed to meet the commitments in the previous agreements between the european communities and the state of israel, which entered into force in 2000 and 2006. on 19 september 2011, negotiations between the commission and israel on the necessary technical adaptations were concluded.
in writing. - i voted in favour of this report because i believe that the protocol on the administration of tariff quotas is a particularly important instrument for the stability and reliability of trade relations. i draw attention to the fact that it is essential to avoid the repetition of the consecutive increases applied by the russian federation to timber export duties. over time, they have affected a large number of union producers. i also believe that the eu has a strong offensive interest in this agreement. he envisages a major improvement in the supply of timber from the russian federation. the agreement is also welcome as it aims to ensure greater predictability as well as better trading conditions.
in writing. - i voted in favour of the report on the conclusion of the agreement in the form of an exchange of letters between the european union and the russian federation on the administration of tariff quotas applying to exports of wood from the russian federation to the european union and of the protocol between the european union and the government of the russian federation on technical modalities adopted pursuant to the said agreement. the russian federation has committed to reduce the levels of export duties it currently applies to raw materials, including raw wood products. the russian federation introduced tariff quotas for certain types of wood, namely wood from certain coniferous species. low export duties are applied to exports from the russian federation for quantities exported within the quota and high, even prohibitive, duties for products not falling within the quota. these quotas have been set at a relatively high level for the eu, at least taking into account the expected short-term demand. this bilateral agreement defines the general provisions for the implementation of the tariff sub-quotas. i welcome the conclusion of the protocol between the eu and the russian federation laying down the detailed technical arrangements for this shared management of tariff quotas.
in writing. − i would like to insist on the crucial role of sis ii in building a europe without borders and increasing the security of the schengen area. i support the commission’s proposal related to the migration from sis 1+ to sis ii. in parallel to its intention to apply the legal framework for sis ii from the moment the first member state completes its switchover to the new system. i welcome the commission’s proposal to provide for the possibility to co-finance certain national activities related to the migration up to 75 %. nevertheless, given the political importance of the issue and its significant budget, i regret that the european parliament is only limited to a consulting role.
in writing. - i voted in favour of the legislative resolution on the draft regulation on the migration from the schengen information system (sis 1+) to the second generation schengen information system (sis ii). the objective of this regulation is to reform regulation (ec) no 1104/2008 and council decision 2008/839/jha into a single legal instrument. this regulation lays down the tasks and responsibilities of the commission and the member states participating in sis 1+ with regard to the maintenance and further development of sis ii, the full testing of sis ii, the testing of supplementary information, the further development and testing of a conversion system, the establishment and testing of a temporary migration structure and the migration from sis 1+ to sis ii. the development of sis ii shall be completed by 30 june 2013 at the latest. bulgaria and romania are taking part in this process in accordance with article 4 (2) of the 2005 act of accession and council decision 2010/365/eu of 29 june 2012 on the application of the provisions of the schengen acquis relating to the schengen information system to the republic of bulgaria and romania. in addition to the recording of automated searches, member states and the commission should ensure that the applicable data protection rules are fully respected during the migration from sis 1+ to sis ii.
in writing. − the european area of freedom, security and justice relies on the schengen information system (sis). with sis ii, the system’s second generation, data will be better secured and shared information used more efficiently. the migration from sis 1+ to sis ii will be challenging and should take place as early as possible. in this respect, i welcome the commission’s proposal to apply the legal framework for sis ii from the moment the first member state completes its switchover to the new system. this will reinforce legal certainty and prevent unnecessary expenses in the member states. however, if we want sis ii to reach its full potential, we must make sure that it receives data of high-quality. prior to the start of the migration from sis 1+ to sis ii, member states must verify that all the personal data to be migrated to sis ii are accurate, up-to-date and lawful in accordance with decision 2007/533/jha. the success of the migration will be determined by the member states’ cooperation.
in writing. − i voted in favour of this report, as i believe that the european parliament has a responsibility to help meet the deadlines for implementing sis ii, as this regulation is part of the migration process to the new schengen information system. the reports on migration to sis ii were adopted in the libe committee by a simplified procedure, in order to make available to the commission and the member states as soon as possible both the legal instruments and the funds necessary for the transition to the new generation of sis. i hope that the commission and the member states will both honour their commitments and fully respect their responsibilities and the timetable for implementing sis ii.
in writing. − in the process of applying european law at member state level, national courts play an important role. to improve this process, it is essential to continue the legal training process of all legal, judicial and administrative authorities on the one hand, but also of the legal professions and national administrations. this constant effort will lead to the respect of the concept of a union based on the rule of law.
in writing. − it is encouraging to read in this report that 88% of the infringement cases completed in 2010 did not reach the court of justice, as member states had remedied the legal problems raised by the commission before the next stage of the infringement procedure was initiated. however, i believe that monitoring of member states should continue as there are many cases where it has been shown that problems reappear after a case has been closed. moreover, the commission should consider the possibility of imposing financial penalties as a measure to ensure compliance with the legislation.
in writing. - i voted in favour of the resolution on the 28th annual report of the commission on monitoring the application of european union law. the environment, the internal market and taxation are the policy areas with the highest risk of non-compliance and account for 52% of all non-compliance findings. we welcome the use by the commission of a large number of tools to facilitate the process of transposition of european legislation into national law (transposition checklists, manuals or information bulletins) and encourage the commission to follow up the transposition of directives before the transposition deadline even more closely, in order to allow for rapid intervention. we emphasise that the petition is the tool that citizens, civil society organisations and businesses can use to inform about the non-compliance with eu law by member state authorities at different levels. national courts play a key role in the application of eu law and fully support eu efforts to improve and coordinate the legal training of legal, judicial and administrative authorities and members of the legal professions, official representatives and officials in national administrations.
in writing. − in order to have an objective view of shale gas and oil extraction, i believe it is important to monitor regulatory mechanisms and practices globally and to address concerns about the environmental effects of extraction. regulation should aim to minimise the impact on the environment and to strike a reasonable balance based on scientific findings and a comprehensive analysis of risks and benefits. the commission and the national competent authorities should continue to study the possible environmental effects, but from a scientific perspective and based on statistics covering reliable sources in the member states and worldwide.
in writing. − studies carried out at the request of the european commission clearly demonstrate that shale gas exploitation poses major risks to the environment and human health. the commission must carry out without delay a detailed assessment of the impact on the environment and human health of the exploration and extraction of shale gas and take, as soon as possible and in accordance with the principles of the existing treaties, all necessary measures to review, supplement and extend the current eu legislation on the environment and health protection. the commission should also, in collaboration with the member states and the competent regulatory authorities, establish a permanent monitoring of activities and developments in this area. although shale gas may seem to be a solution to the current energy crisis, it is not a solution for the future. efforts and investments should be channelled towards increasing the share of renewable energy and energy efficiency. only 'clean' energy, based on 100% renewable energy, gives us a chance to protect our environment, climate, health and resources.
in writing. - i voted for the resolution on the environmental impact of shale gas and shale oil extraction activities, as shale gas exploitation requires a thorough examination of all effects (on the environment, public health and climate change) before further development of this technology. governments in europe, such as those of france, bulgaria, the german state of north rhine-westphalia, the swiss cantons of fribourg and vaud, and a number of u.s. states have instituted a ban or moratorium on the use of hydraulic fracturing to extract oil and shale gas. i voted for amendment no 5, which, on the basis of the precautionary principle and the principle of preventive action, taking into account the risks and negative effects on the climate, the environment and health of hydraulic fracturing and the gaps identified in the regulatory framework in the eu for shale gas activities, urges member states not to authorise any new hydraulic fracturing operations in the eu. i voted in favour of calling for a ban on hydraulic fracturing in certain vulnerable and high-risk areas, for example in protected drinking water reserves and underground, and in coal mining areas.
in writing. − i voted in favour of the report on industrial, energy and other aspects of shale gas and oil. shale gas is a big opportunity for all member states; it is a challenge. it is an opportunity to make member states more independent from major suppliers. of course shale gas has some environmental risk; this is why it is very important to have rules and follow them. we should definitely regulate the method and technique of extraction of shale gas with proper legislation. this is an opportunity to achieve growth and to be more competitive with the rest of the world. it is a big step that we need to take, taking into account all the environmental risks.
in writing. - i voted in favour of the resolution on industrial, energy and other aspects of shale gas and shale oil. i believe that decision-makers should have accurate, up-to-date and comprehensive scientific data at their disposal to enable them to make informed choices in this area. europe's potential for the extraction and use of shale gas and shale oil resources must be assessed and inventoried without compromising the availability and quality of water resources. we believe that no exploration or exploitation of shale gas should take place unless there are guarantees that there are no risks to the environment and to the surrounding communities. i voted against paragraphs 15 and 27, which argued that shale gas contributes to the eu's target of reducing greenhouse gas emissions by 80-95% by 2050. at present, there are no conclusive studies in this direction. we call on member states to establish a robust regulatory regime and to provide the necessary administrative and monitoring resources for the development of shale gas activities. it is recalled that, in accordance with the principle of subsidiarity, each member state has the right to adopt decisions on the exploitation of oil and shale gas.
in writing. − the commission's intensive work to encourage citizens' active participation in the decision-making process within the european union is welcome, and the increase in the number of petitions filed in 2011 by almost 20% compared to 2010 shows that citizens are interested in directly contributing to important decisions at the level of the eu institutions. i am concerned, however, that about 30% of petitions have been declared inadmissible, which indicates that people are not yet sufficiently well informed to strictly comply with all eligibility requirements, and this can only be remedied by intensive campaigns of correct and complete education and information in the territory. on the other hand, as regards the fields of application, it is worth noting the significant increase in the number of petitions submitted on environmental issues, which shows an intensification of citizens' concern in this regard, but at the same time, signals the existence of serious problems in the management of projects that cause damage to the environment.
in writing. − i voted in favour of the report on the activities of the committee on petitions in 2011. the committee on petitions has an obligation to constantly review and strengthen its role, especially in relation to the development of democratic principles, such as increased citizen participation in the eu decision-making process and enhanced transparency and accountability. in the course of its normal work, the committee works closely with the member states, the commission, the european ombudsman and other bodies to ensure that the spirit and the letter of union law are fully respected. i would point out the increasing number of petitions and other requests from citizens seeking legal and financial redress on matters outside the area of competence conferred on the eu, such as requests for the revision of the method of calculating national pensions and the annulment of judgments handed down by national courts, proposals to change the borders of europe, etc. we welcome the parliament's decision to develop a more practical and visible petition portal on its website, which will facilitate citizens' access to the petition process, provide them with information and allow them to present petitions in a more user-friendly environment that allows for the electronic signing of petitions.
president-in-office of the council. − mr president, we very much regret that the conciliation committee which was convened after the european parliament’s last plenary session in october 2012 was not able to reach agreement on a joint text on the 2013 budget within the 21-day period foreseen by the treaty. the cyprus presidency did its utmost to achieve a positive outcome within the given timeframe. we worked hard to try to reconcile positions right up to the last few hours. but in the end we had to accept that the views of our two institutions remained far apart, and that it was therefore unfortunately not possible to reach an agreement. the council believes that it showed considerable openness throughout the negotiations, and in particular during the last few days of the conciliation period. it was able to make some progress, and specifically was able to approve one of the key elements of the negotiation package – the draft amending budget no 5 for 2012 related to the mobilisation of eur 670 million from the eu solidarity fund in support of italy – without any modifications to the commission’s proposal. despite this, we were not able to find the necessary flexibility in each of our institutions needed to make further progress on the 2013 budget. the mandate given to the conciliation committee was to find an agreement on the 2013 budget. however, it proved impossible to find a way forward on this issue without having addressed first the issue of the draft amending budget no 6 for 2012, which seeks eur 9 billion in additional payment appropriations for this year. ms gardiazábal rubial is right that erasmus and globalisation are part of draft amending budget no 6 and we understand and appreciate the sense of urgency. the council was and is ready to discuss all elements of the budgetary package and is committed to honouring our payment obligations, but we continue to take the view that they cannot be dealt with in isolation from each other if we are to find a balanced outcome which will meet the concerns of all parties. this was in fact the hiatus between our respective positions. for us, there is an inescapable link between draft amending budget no 6 for 2012 and the 2013 budget, since both of them aim at ensuring the continuity of the same european union programmes and actions, and both of them have to be financed from the same contributions from the member states. of course, having said that, it has to be very clear that we fully honour and respect the rights and prerogatives of parliament and the essence and the nature of the budgetary procedure (i.e., colegislation, codecision); there is even an edge in your favour under some specific circumstances. we now have only a few weeks left until the end of this year. we now of course await, as was said, a new draft budget from the commission which will need to take due account of the progress we have made to date in reconciling the different positions of our two institutions. clearly, i would have preferred to have been in a different situation to that which we find ourselves in today. but i remain hopeful that we can still reach a positive outcome in the short time that is left to us. the cyprus presidency will do its utmost to make rapid progress on the basis of the new draft budget. we count on parliament’s willingness to engage in a constructive dialogue so that we can have an eu budget in place from the beginning of the year. i am convinced that our collective credibility would be at stake if we failed to deliver this time round. it would simply not be understood if we were unable to reach agreement given what is at stake. but i am convinced that we can overcome the difficulties and reach a compromise. the cyprus presidency – and i personally – am committed to delivering a successful outcome.

rapporteur. − mr president, europe has never been so prosperous, so secure, nor so free. words written in the european security strategy of 2003 are questionable today, confronted with increasingly complex risks and threats moving closer and closer to home. to those, we answer with a rush to slash our defence budgets, making life miserable for the defence planners, be they from nato or the eu. moreover, nato, responsible for the security of 21 of the 27 eu member states, is confronted with the american reorientation towards asia, forcing europe to manage the consequences through increasing their contribution to nato and strengthening the eu security and defence dimension. this report is a step in that latter direction. to that effect, under the existing legal reality, the report does not ask for new instruments or new powers for the eu but argues for a more coherent and efficient interaction of the existing instruments, pointing to what the union should do in case either one or both clauses are invoked, apart from and until the national mechanisms are activated. this way, the eu mechanisms do not substitute for the national ones. they only support and amend them, helping the member states to deal successfully with a situation invoking the clauses. in other words, the report is about solidarity. any member of the eu, including those not in nato, is entitled to respect from their organisation because solidarity is indispensable to the cohesion of the eu, acting as a deterrent of aggression too; particularly at a time when, due to the current crisis, centrifugal forces are getting stronger. although in practice the two clauses, mutual defence and solidarity, could be interconnected, the report takes them separately for reasons of clarity. what the report names the mutual defence clause – because in the treaty on european union it is nameless – although it deals with measures in case of external armed aggression is a provision imported from the treaty of brussels establishing the western european union, which after lisbon has been embedded into the eu’s legal basis. on the other hand, the solidarity clause is an addition following the multiplication of natural and man-made disasters both within and outside the eu. since article 42(7) states that the eu nato members rely for their security on the north atlantic treaty, the report underlines the importance of the relationship between the eu and nato which should be seen as cooperative and not competitive, being instead organisations complementary to one another. to that effect, the report advocates the cohesion of the eu’s pooling and sharing and nato’s smart defence initiatives; the creation in time of an eu headquarters; and defining today’s risks and threats in a modern way, adapted to reality. in turn, the solidarity clause is meant to address the situations where the national capacities of a state to deal with a certain disaster are overwhelmed, to maintain a balance between preparedness and flexibility and to avoid the phenomenon of free riding when one prefers to rely more on others than on oneself. the report, arguing for the best use of such instruments like the civil protection mechanism, the internal security strategy and the capacities of the external action service, supports the ongoing review of the emergency and crisis coordination arrangement and the development of an integrated situational awareness. in conclusion, the report asks the high representative to propose practical arrangements and guidelines for ensuring a rapid and coherent response in the event of a member state invoking the mutual defence clause. we also call on the commission and the high representative before the end of 2012 to make the joint proposal for a council decision, defining the arrangements for the implementation of the solidarity clause, clarifying in particular the roles and competences of different actors.
in congratulating the four rapporteurs, i cannot but express my regret, because each report deserves a debate. each report adds value to our common security and defence policy. i will speak of principle, saying that the treaty of lisbon gives this common policy a chance, legally speaking. we must no longer doubt this opportunity, but we must doubt our ability to implement it, because it is not possible, even though a few years have passed since we came under the treaty and since we are talking about more europe or a better governed europe, not to give operationality to the clauses to which we have committed ourselves. this weakens the union's position as a relevant actor in both foreign policy and global security. if we want more union, more europe, we must give a major chance to the common security and defence policy, not to judge things by sector, as has unfortunately happened today.
mr president, i am pleased that my amendment on considering the need for the eu to develop a ‘white hat’ strategy was adopted by the committee responsible. with cyber criminals getting better at breaking into protected networks, i strongly believe that the only real way to win the battle is to have people with similar knowledge and expertise fighting against them. i would remind you of some statistics: more than one million people become victims of cyber crime every day, and the cost of cyber crime, as estimated by the commission, could reach a total of usd 388 billion worldwide. therefore, as i have stated in all my speeches, i believe ‘white hat’ hackers need to be hired and trained for future cyber warfare.
i'd like to refer to mr. kelam's report. the communication and information technology infrastructure is part of the european critical infrastructure. many cyber incidents occur due to the lack of resilience and robustness of private and public network infrastructure, weakly secured databases and other critical information infrastructure failures. we call on member states to develop national cybersecurity and defence strategies, train engineers to protect information systems and invest in cybersecurity research and innovation. enisa shall support member states through the exchange of best practices in the field of cybersecurity and in the development, implementation and maintenance of national cybersecurity strategies. the commission is also proposing to extend the scope of the directive to include the protection of the environment and the environmentally friendly use of energy. we ask the council and the commission to be flexible in this respect, otherwise enisa's current mandate expires in september 2013.
the lisbon treaty gave the union new instruments for external action, which strengthened its international profile. within the framework of security and defence policy, it is possible to organise civil or military missions in sensitive areas. although there have been missions in areas such as chad, the congo, somalia, the union has not been sufficiently involved in the frozen conflicts on its borders. the conflict in transnistria, which has lasted for more than 20 years, is the best example. although there were high expectations from the new leadership in tiraspol, they were dashed after the first rounds of negotiations, and the political commitment to make progress in resolving the conflict proved to be insincere. that is why i believe that the union, through the high representative, should be more involved in resolving the conflict by replacing the military peacekeeping mission with a civilian one.
